title: Commercial Shipping – Who's Who
introduction: Commercial shipping is a global business involving many different organizations, each with specific responsibilities. Some companies own ships, others operate them, while others arrange cargo, insurance, legal services or port operations. Understanding who does what is essential for anyone working in the maritime industry. Although these parties often work together, each has its own contractual responsibilities and commercial interests.

sections.title: 1. Introduction to Commercial Shipping
paragraphs: A merchant vessel is much more than just a ship at sea. Behind every voyage is a network of companies responsible for financing, operating, maintaining, chartering, insuring and supplying the vessel.

Modern commercial shipping relies on cooperation between technical specialists, commercial operators, legal advisors, insurers and cargo interests. Each voyage involves contracts between several independent companies.

sections.title: 2. The Shipowner
paragraphs: The shipowner is the legal owner of the vessel. The owner invests in the ship and is ultimately responsible for its registration, insurance and long-term operation.
Many owners do not operate their own vessels directly. Instead, they hire professional ship management companies.

sections.title: 3. Ship Management Companies
paragraphs: A ship management company operates the vessel on behalf of the owner. Depending on the contract, it may provide technical management, crewing, purchasing, budgeting and regulatory compliance.
Large companies such as Noatum CSM manage fleets for many different owners.

sections.title: 4. Charterers
paragraphs: A charterer hires the use of a vessel rather than owning it. Different charter agreements allocate responsibilities differently.
Understanding the differences between voyage, time and bareboat charters is fundamental in commercial shipping.
points: Voyage Charter – hires the vessel for one voyage.
Time Charter – hires the vessel for a period of time.
Bareboat Charter – hires the vessel without crew and assumes most operational responsibilities.

sections.title: 5. Cargo Interests
paragraphs: Cargo interests are the parties involved with the goods being transported. They include those sending, buying and receiving the cargo.

sections.title: 6. Ship Brokers
paragraphs: Ship brokers act as intermediaries between shipowners and charterers. They do not usually own ships or cargo themselves.
Their role is to negotiate charter parties, freight rates and commercial terms.

sections.title: 7. Freight Forwarders
paragraphs: Freight forwarders coordinate the transportation of cargo using ships, trucks, trains and aircraft.
Unlike brokers, freight forwarders focus on the logistics chain rather than chartering vessels.

sections.title: 8. Port and Liner Agents
paragraphs: A Port Agent represents the vessel during a port call. The agent coordinates pilotage, towage, customs clearance, berth arrangements and local services.
A Liner Agent represents a shipping line and often handles bookings, customer service and documentation.

sections.title: 9. Marine Insurance
paragraphs: Marine insurance is generally divided into Hull & Machinery insurance and Protection & Indemnity insurance.
Together they protect both the physical ship and the owner's legal liabilities.
points: Hull & Machinery (H&M) covers physical damage to the vessel.
Protection & Indemnity (P&I) covers liabilities including pollution, cargo claims and crew injuries.

sections.title: 10. Marine Surveyors
paragraphs: Marine surveyors are independent experts who inspect ships or cargo. Their reports are often used by insurers, owners and courts.

sections.title: 11. Maritime Lawyers
paragraphs: Maritime lawyers specialize in shipping law and resolve disputes involving charter parties, cargo claims, collisions, pollution, salvage and insurance.

sections.title: 12. How They Work Together
paragraphs: Consider a shipment of iron ore from Brazil to Japan. A trader sells the cargo to a steel manufacturer. The trader charters a bulk carrier through a ship broker. The vessel is owned by one company but technically managed by another. A port agent arranges arrival formalities in Brazil and Japan. The freight forwarder coordinates inland transport. If damage occurs, a surveyor investigates while the P&I Club and maritime lawyers assist with any resulting claims.

keyPoint: Commercial shipping depends on cooperation between many independent organizations. Understanding each party's responsibilities is essential for understanding how the maritime industry operates.
commonMistake: Many people confuse the shipowner with the ship manager. The owner legally owns the vessel, while the ship manager may operate it on the owner's behalf. Likewise, a freight forwarder coordinates logistics but does not normally charter or operate ships like a ship broker.
summary: Ship Managers operate vessels for owners.
Port Agents handle local port operations.
Commercial shipping is built on contracts between all these parties.
